facts.statehood_note: Arkansas joined the Union at the same time as Michigan: under the Missouri Compromise, a new slave state was paired with a new free state.
facts.motto: Regnat Populus (Latin for "The people rule"), adopted 1907
facts.name_origin: French explorers called the Quapaw people the "Arkansas," from an Illini word meaning "People of the South Wind," and the name spread to the river and the land. In 1881 the legislature made the final "s" silent by law.

government.legislature: Arkansas General Assembly (meets at the Arkansas State Capitol in Little Rock)
government.chambers: Arkansas Senate (35 members, 4-year terms) and Arkansas House of Representatives (100 members, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term since Amendment 63 in 1984; limited to two terms since 1992). The governor enforces state laws, leads the state militia, appoints the 15 secretaries who run Cabinet departments, signs or vetoes bills, and can veto single lines of spending bills. A simple majority of the General Assembly can override a veto. The Lieutenant Governor is the governor's deputy.
government.courts: Arkansas Supreme Court (7 justices: a chief justice and six associate justices) is the highest court. Justices are chosen in nonpartisan elections for staggered 8-year terms; if a seat opens mid-term, the governor appoints someone to fill it.
government.constitution: The current constitution was ratified in 1874, after the Brooks-Baxter War. Arkansas had earlier constitutions in 1836, 1861, 1864, and 1868 (the Reconstruction constitution). It had 102 amendments as of 2020.
government.kid_line: "The equality of all persons before the law is recognized, and shall ever remain inviolate" (Arkansas Constitution, Article 2, Section 3)

long_ago.about: People first lived in what is now Arkansas around 11,500 BCE. Over thousands of years, later peoples began building mounds, farming, living in large villages, and trading over long distances.
From about 650 to 1050 CE, the Plum Bayou people built as many as 18 mounds around two plazas; one mound is almost 50 feet high. They grew squash and sunflowers and held large feasts at the mounds.

long_ago.nation: Casqui people (ancestors of the Quapaw Nation)
long_ago.about: The town at today's Parkin was the center of a large chiefdom from about 1350 to 1600. Hernando de Soto's Spanish expedition met the Casqui people there, and Spanish trade goods have been found at the site.

In 1673 the Quapaw lived in four villages along the Mississippi and Arkansas rivers. Women farmed maize, squash, and beans, men hunted deer, bears, and bison, and families lived in longhouses around a central plaza; the nation had two divisions, Earth and Sky, with 21 clans.
The Caddo lived in southern Arkansas and were known for building mounds.
The Osage lived in Missouri but claimed large parts of Arkansas as hunting lands. An 1808 treaty took Osage land claims in Arkansas.

first_peoples.today_note: Treaties and forced removals in the 1800s pushed the Quapaw, Osage, Cherokee, Choctaw, and other nations out of Arkansas. The Quapaw Nation is headquartered today in Quapaw, Oklahoma, and most members live in northeastern Oklahoma. When Arkansas renamed Toltec Mounds as Plum Bayou Mounds, it consulted the Quapaw and Osage Nations.
sites: Plum Bayou Mounds Archeological State Park (once called Toltec Mounds; a National Historic Landmark)
Parkin Archeological State Park (center of a chiefdom from 1350 to 1600, where de Soto met the Casqui people)
Davidsonville Historic State Park (Arkansas's first county seat, with Archaic period artifacts from 8500 to 1000 BCE)

history.event: Paleoindian peoples are the first people to live in what is now Arkansas.
The Plum Bayou people build a mound center with as many as 18 mounds and two large plazas.
Hernando de Soto's Spanish expedition enters Arkansas, bringing disease and violence; at Parkin the Spanish meet the Casqui people.
French explorers led by Father Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet meet the Quapaw, who live in four villages along the Mississippi and Arkansas rivers.
Arkansas Post is founded; it serves France, and later Spain, for more than a century.
The United States buys the region in the Louisiana Purchase, and on March 23, 1804, a U.S. Army officer takes control of Arkansas Post.
Congress creates Arkansas Territory on March 2, 1819, and on June 1, 1821, the capital moves from Arkansas Post to Little Rock.

Treaties take Quapaw land; after a forced move to the Red River in Louisiana brings floods and hunger, the Quapaw return and are removed to Indian Territory in 1833. An 1828 treaty forces the Arkansas Cherokee, including Sequoyah, to trade their land for land in today's Oklahoma.
The U.S. government forces Choctaw, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, and Cherokee people west across Arkansas to Indian Territory; the Cherokee Trail of Tears passes in 1838 to 1839.
Arkansas becomes the 25th state on June 15, admitted as a slave state alongside the free state of Michigan.

Arkansas enslavers hold 111,115 African Americans in slavery, about one in four people in the state; in Chicot County about 78 percent of people are enslaved. Enslaved people resist in many ways, including running away.

Arkansas votes to leave the Union on May 6, 1861, and joins the Confederacy. Union armies win at Pea Ridge and Prairie Grove in northwest Arkansas, and Little Rock falls to Union troops in September 1863.

Under Reconstruction, Arkansas writes a new constitution and is restored to the Union in June. Freedpeople gain political power and many Black Arkansans hold state and city offices, while the Ku Klux Klan fights these changes with violence.

Mifflin Gibbs becomes Little Rock's police judge, called the first elected Black municipal judge in the U.S. After the Brooks-Baxter War of 1874, Democrats return to power and a new state constitution is ratified.

trailblazers.name: Sequoyah
trailblazers.group: Cherokee man, inventor of the Cherokee writing system
trailblazers.text: Sequoyah created a written form of the Cherokee language, and in 1824 the Cherokee Council honored him with a medal for it. By 1824 he lived in Arkansas near Illinois Bayou in Pope County, and in 1828 he was part of the delegation that traded the Cherokee's Arkansas lands for land in today's northeast Oklahoma. He later helped form the Cherokee Nation in 1839.

trailblazers.name: Mifflin Wistar Gibbs
trailblazers.group: Black American man, lawyer and judge
trailblazers.text: Born in Philadelphia, Mifflin Gibbs came to Little Rock in 1871 and passed the bar in 1872. He won the Republican nomination for Little Rock police judge in 1873 and served from 1874 to 1875, becoming the first elected African American municipal judge in the United States. He later served as U.S. consul to Madagascar and in 1903 founded a Black-owned bank in Little Rock.

trailblazers.name: Hattie Caraway
trailblazers.text: Hattie Caraway of Jonesboro was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 1931 after her husband died. On January 12, 1932, she became the first woman ever elected to the U.S. Senate, and she was the first woman to preside over the Senate and to chair a Senate committee. She served until 1945.

trailblazers.name: Daisy Bates
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, journalist and civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: Raised in Huttig, Daisy Bates and her husband, L. C. Bates, started the Arkansas State Press newspaper in Little Rock in 1941. As president of the Arkansas NAACP, she mentored the Little Rock Nine, the nine Black students at the center of Little Rock's school desegregation in 1957. Her statue was placed in the U.S. Capitol in 2024.

trailblazers.name: Edith Irby Jones
trailblazers.text: In 1948 Edith Irby Jones, whose hometown was Hot Springs, became the first Black student at the University of Arkansas School of Medicine, and she earned her medical degree in 1952. In 1985 she became the first woman elected president of the National Medical Association.

trailblazers.name: Paul Kazuo Kuroda
trailblazers.text: Born in Japan in 1917, Paul Kuroda joined the University of Arkansas in Fayetteville as a chemistry professor in 1952 and taught there until he retired in 1987. He predicted that nuclear reactors could form naturally inside the Earth nearly twenty years before scientists found the first one, in uranium ore traced to the Oklo mines in Gabon, Africa, after 1972. In 1979 he became the university's first Edgar Wertheim Distinguished Professor of Chemistry.

landforms: Ouachita Mountains (from near Little Rock into Oklahoma; home of Hot Springs)
Crowley's Ridge (higher ground running about 150 miles through the Delta)
Mississippi Alluvial Plain, or the Delta (the eastern third of the state)
West Gulf Coastal Plain (most of southern Arkansas)
waters: Ouachita River (lowest point, 56 feet, at the Louisiana border)
Bull Shoals Lake and Lake Ouachita (reservoirs)
geography.regions: Arkansas has two highland regions, the Ozark Plateau and the Ouachita Mountains, with the Arkansas River Valley between them, and two lowland regions, the Mississippi Alluvial Plain (Delta) in the east and the West Gulf Coastal Plain in the south, with Crowley's Ridge rising out of the Delta.

ecosystems.name: Ozark and Ouachita forests
ecosystems.about: Forests cover about 56% of Arkansas. Oak, hickory, shortleaf pine, and loblolly pine are the main trees, and the white-tailed deer is the state mammal.

ecosystems.name: Crowley's Ridge
ecosystems.about: This long ridge of higher ground through the flat Delta is the only place in Arkansas where the tulip tree grows naturally.

ecosystems.name: The Delta (Mississippi Alluvial Plain)
ecosystems.about: The flat, rich soil of eastern Arkansas is farm country, where rice, soybeans, and cotton grow and catfish are raised.

ecosystems.name: Hot springs of the Ouachitas
ecosystems.about: The hot springs in the Ouachita Mountains form when groundwater is heated far below the surface and flows back up.

science.weather: Arkansas has a humid subtropical climate with frequent thunderstorms, tornadoes, hail, ice storms, and occasional snow; it lies in "Dixie Alley," near Tornado Alley. River flooding is a hazard too, as in the Great Mississippi Flood of 1927.
science.resources: Arkansas grows rice, soybeans, and cotton, raises catfish, and is the nation's largest producer of broiler chickens and turkeys. It also produces timber, natural gas, oil, and bromine, and bauxite was once important.
science.highlight: Crater of Diamonds State Park near Murfreesboro in Pike County is a place where diamonds are found in the ground, which is why the diamond became the state gem in 1967.

g3_ss.title: Arkansas's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Little Rock and Arkansas's 75 counties; learn what the governor, the 135-member General Assembly, and the 7-justice Supreme Court do; read "Regnat Populus" (The people rule) and Article 2, Section 3 on equality.

g3_ss.title: Arkansas's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Visit (in photos) Plum Bayou Mounds and Parkin, and learn how the Quapaw, the "People of the South Wind," farmed and lived in longhouses, and where the Quapaw Nation lives today.

g3_ss.title: Arkansas Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make trading cards for Sequoyah, Mifflin Gibbs, Hattie Caraway, Daisy Bates, and Edith Irby Jones, and tell what "first" each one achieved.

g45_ss.title: Arkansas's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Trace people from 11,500 BCE through the Plum Bayou mound builders and the Casqui chiefdom to the Quapaw, Caddo, and Osage, then follow the treaties and removals of the 1800s.

g45_ss.title: Colonial and Territorial Arkansas
g45_ss.plan: Follow de Soto (1541), Marquette and Jolliet (1673), Arkansas Post (1686), the Louisiana Purchase, Arkansas Territory (1819), and the Trail of Tears across Arkansas.

g45_ss.title: Arkansas 1836 to 1874
g45_ss.plan: Study statehood as a slave state, the lives and resistance of enslaved people, secession and Civil War battles, and Reconstruction, when Black Arkansans like Mifflin Gibbs won office, through the Brooks-Baxter War.

g3_sci.title: Arkansas Forests
g3_sci.plan: Identify oak, hickory, and pine leaves and cones, and list animals like white-tailed deer that depend on the forest.

g3_sci.title: Storm Safety
g3_sci.plan: Learn how thunderstorms, tornadoes, hail, and ice storms form, and practice a tornado safety plan.

g3_sci.title: Diamonds and Rocks
g3_sci.plan: Sort rocks and minerals (diamond, quartz, bauxite) by properties like hardness and shine, connecting to Crater of Diamonds State Park.

g45_sci.title: Hot Springs and Groundwater
g45_sci.plan: Model how rain soaks deep underground, gets heated, and rises again as hot springs in the Ouachita Mountains.

g45_sci.title: Landforms of Arkansas
g45_sci.plan: Build a relief map of the Ozarks, Ouachitas, Arkansas Valley, Delta, and Crowley's Ridge, and compare highest and lowest points.

g45_sci.title: Rivers, Floods, and Farms
g45_sci.plan: Investigate how the Mississippi and Arkansas rivers built the Delta's rich soil, why floods like 1927 happen, and how rice and catfish farms use water.
